title: Empire
full_review:
A know-it-all drug dealer meets a predictable fate in the awful "Empire" (Universal).

Featuring an atrociously written script from Franc. Reyes, who also directed, the tired device of a voiceover opens the tale. Victor (John Leguizamo) brags about how he has the brains to survive being a filthy-rich drug dealer -- the South Bronx's answer to Bill Gates. Again and again he drones on about how money is everything. Not a moment's thought does he give to how the drug trade ruins lives, nor does he spare the lives of anyone who gets in his way.

However, his safety is compromised when a turf war breaks out. Victor executes rival Tito (Fat Joe) and this angers their mutual supplier (Isabella Rossellini).

When Carmen (Delilah Cotto), Victor's live-in girlfriend, announces she's pregnant, he decides it's time to quit the drug trade. Carmen's pal (Denise Richards) introduces him to her investment banker boyfriend (Peter Sarsgaard) who promises incredible returns. Victor hands him a million dollars, which the investor quickly doubles. Now Victor's greedy supplier wants in so they pony up over $5 million -- and the banker takes a powder.

The script insults the intelligence of viewers with plot holes larger than Victor's ego. Every so often there are shootouts whose bullets blow holes in the wall so big you could throw a basketball through them, and the accidental murder of a child is only worth a shrug. Both Victor and the banker get to rationalize constantly about the unimportance of pushing drugs as long as you can make a fortune.

The supposed glamour of materialism is on full display as Victor and his live-in decorate their posh Soho loft and she doesn't mind wearing diamonds bought from drug profits. While Leguizamo is credible as the cocky drug lord, it's distressing that accomplished actresses such as Rossellini and Sonia Braga as Carmen's mom are reduced to appearing in such a trashy time-waster.

Reyes' visuals are self-consciously high style and glossy but, with such a heavy-handed and far-fetched narrative peopled by across-the-board despicable characters, "Empire" should claim no territory at the box-office.

Due to intense violence, rationalization of crime, sexual situations with nudity, a few instances of profanity and nonstop rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive.
